say.text: Before I teach anything, let me see what you already carry. A baby is brought in looking blue.
Which is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the stem again. It gives no age and no qualifier, so pick the answer an unqualified 'most common' stem is built on.
Transposition is a famous blue-baby lesion, so it comes to mind quickly. But this stem has no age qualifier, and that changes which lesion it keys.
Re-read it once more and choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so slow down on superlatives: check for a qualifier before you commit.

say.text: Same stem, second look. Which is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?
Here is the key. An unqualified stem keys **Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)**: it is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease.
Separate idea: TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate. 'Commonest' and 'usually presents as' are two different statements.
Yes. TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, and its picture varies with how severe the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction is.
Now recall the anatomy. This is a classic exam stem.
Which of these is NOT a component of classic TOF?
Hypertrophy sounds like an add-on, so it is easy to doubt. But think about which side of the heart has to work against the obstruction.
Does that side thicken or not? Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: ask which ventricle faces the load.

say.text: 'Infundibular' sounds like a different site from the valve, so it can look like the odd one out. But a name you rarely hear is not the same as a lesion that is absent.
Think about where the narrowing sits, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the unfamiliar word may be the true one.

say.text: 'Overriding' is a vivid word that can sound like a complication rather than a defining feature. Ask whether it is part of the malformation itself.
Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: vivid does not mean optional.

say.text: Second look. Which is NOT one of the four components of classic TOF?
The four are a large, anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among the four. PYQs keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'.
Right. The four are a large, anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy; ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among them.

choices.label: I know this, skip the recap

say.text: PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'. Current StatPearls lists the four as a VSD, an overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
One last gate. A child has TOF, but the resistance across the RVOT is less than the systemic vascular resistance.
How will the child look?

choices.label: Deeply cyanotic from birth, as in every TOF
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Blood takes the easier road. Compare the two resistances in the stem and ask which way blood prefers to go.
'Tetralogy means blue' is a strong shortcut, so this is tempting. But it ignores what the stem actually gave you: how the two resistances compare.
Use that comparison and choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: let the resistances decide, not the label.

say.text: Resistance across the RVOT is below systemic vascular resistance. How does the child look?

choices.label: Deeply cyanotic, because every TOF is blue

say.text: If resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic vascular resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
So TOF does not always mean blue: severity of RVOT obstruction sets the picture.
Yes. Lower resistance across the RVOT than systemic resistance means minimally cyanotic or acyanotic, which fits a presentation that varies with RVOT obstruction.
That was your starting map. Where you hesitated is where we build next: one malaligned septum, and why the four components follow from it.
